questions.solution:
Diameter of each rivet ( D )=6  mm

∴ Radius (r) = D 2 = 3 mm = 3 × 10 - 3 m

Maximum shearing stress on each rivet = 6.9 × 107 Pa

Let w be the maximum load that can be subjected to the riveted strip.
As each rivet carry one-quarter of the load, therefore

Load on each rivet = w 4

Maximum shearing stress = Maximum shearing force Area            

∴ 6.9 × 10 7 = w / 4 π r 2

or w=6.9× 10 7  4 πr 2

​or w=6.9× 10 7 ×4×3.1 4× ( 3× 10 −3 ) 2

=6.9×4×3.14×9×10

=7.8× 10 3  N

If the volume strain produced in the sphere after charging is x×10-11, then the value of x is
questions.solution:
Bulk modulus is given by

B=-ΔPΔVV

The outward electrostatic pressure is

Pelectrostatic=σ22ε0=-ΔP

⇒ΔVV=σ22ε0B

⇒ΔVV=αε022ε02×1011=0.25×10-11

questions.solution:
The acceleration of the rod is

a=Fm

So, the tension in the rod at a distance x from the free end is

Tx=mxl×Fm=Fxl

The longitudinal stress developed inside the rod at a distance x from the free end is

σ=TxA=FxlA

The strain energy density (energy per unit volume) is

dUdV=12σ2Y=12F2x2YA2l2, where dV=Adx is the volume of a small part of the rod

So the energy stored in the rod is

U=12F2YA2l2∫0lx2dx

U=F2l6A2Y

questions.q: Two blocks of masses 5 kg and 10 kg are connected by a metal wire going over a smooth pulley as shown in the figure. The breaking stress of the metal wire is 2×109 N m-2. If g=10 m s-2, then what is the minimum radius of the wire which will not break
questions.solution:
This is Atwood's machine. Let the tension in the wire be T and acceleration of masses a.

questions.q: A load of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>31</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>4</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> is suspended from a wire of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> and density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>9</mn><mo> </mo><mo>×</mo><mo> </mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></math>. Calculate the change in temperature of the wire if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>75</mn><mo>%</mo></math> of the stored elastic potential energy is converted into heat. The Young's modulus and heat capacity of the material of the wire is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>9</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>8</mn><mo> </mo><mo>×</mo><mo> </mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>10</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>490</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi>kg</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> respectively.
options: 4.33 × 10-2 K
8.33 × 10-3 K
2.44 × 10-5 K
6.22 × 10-2 K
questions.solution:
As work done in stretching an elastic body per unit volume is given by

      W V = 1 2 stress × strain = 1 2 stress 2 Y as Y = stress strain    ........ (1)

So W = 1 2 Mg A 2 V Y   as stress = F A = Mg A

Now according to given problem heat produced H = (75/100)  W = 3 4 .W

⇒   ms Δ θ = 3 4 × 1 2 Mg π r 2 2 V Y as H = ms Δ θ using equation (1)

or ρ V s Δ θ = 3 4 × 1 2 Mg π r 2 2 V Y as m = ρ V

∴ Δ θ = 3 8 3 1 . 4 × 9 . 8 π × 1 0 - 6 2 1 9 . 8 × 1 0 1 0 × 1 9 × 1 0 3 × 4 9 0

i.e.,  Δ θ = 1 1 2 0 K = 8 . 3 3 × 1 0 - 3  K

The change of temperature required to produce the same elongation, if the steel rod is heated, is (The modulus of elasticity is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>11</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math> and the coefficient of linear expansion of steel is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>.1</mo><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">℃</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>)
questions.solution:
Modulus of elasticity = ForceArea×l∆l

3×1011 =3300010-3×l∆l

∆ll   =3300010-3×13×1011

=11×10-5

Change in length, ∆ll=α∆T

11×10-5 = 1.1×10-5×∆T

A massless piston of area <math><mi>A</mi></math> floats on the surface of the liquid. When a mass <math><mi>M</mi></math> is placed on the piston to compress the liquid, the fractional change in the radius of the sphere is
questions.solution:
Change in pressure due to placing of mass on piston is,

∆p=MgA

From Bulk modulus definition

K= −Δp ΔV

⇒∆VV=∆pK=MgAK

From  V=43πr3

∆VV=3∆RR

⇒ ∆RR=13∆VV

=Mg3AK

questions.q: Two wires of diameter 0.25 cm, one made of steel and other made of brass are loaded as shown in figure. The unloaded length of steel wire is 1.5 m and that of brass wire is 1.0 m. Young's modulus of steel is 2.0 × 1011 and Young's modulus  of Brass 0.91 × 1011 Pa. The elongations of steel and brass wires are respectively
questions.solution:
Given, diameter of wires (2r) = 0.25 cm

r = 0.125 cm = 1.25 × 10-3 m

For steel wire,

Load (F1) = (4 + 6) kgf = 10 × 9.8 N = 98 N

Length of steel wire (l1) = 1.5 m

Young's modulus (Y1) = 2.0 × 1011 Pa

Young's modulus (Y) = F 1 × l⁡ 1 A 1 × Δ l⁡ 1

Change in length Δ l⁡ 1 = F 1 × l⁡ 1 A 1 × Y 1

= F 1 × l⁡ 1 π r 1 2 × Y 1

= 98 × 1.5 3.14 × 1.25 × 10 - 3 2 × 2.0 × 10 11

​= 1.5 × 10-4 m

For brass wire,

Load (F2) = 6 kgf = 6 × 9.8 N = 58.8 N

Length of brass wire (l2) = 1.0 m

Young's modulus (Y2) = 0.91 × 1011 Pa

Change in length l⁡ 2 = F 2 × l⁡ 2 π r 2 2 × Y 2

= 58.8 × 1.0 3.14 × 1.25 × 10 - 3 2 × 0.91 × 10 11

​ = 1.3 × 10-4 m

If the angular speed is increased to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msqrt><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msqrt><mo> </mo><mi>rad</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>, how much area (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>cm</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>) of the bottom of the vessel is now exposed to surrounding? [Area of the cross-section of cylinder is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>27</mn><mo> </mo><msup><mi>cm</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>]
questions.solution:
Let ω1 be initial angular velocity

ω12R22g=h
For angular velocity ω2 let radius of exposed surface be x

ω222gR2-x2=h
Putting the value of ω1 and ω2
πx2=9
Since πR2=27

questions.q: A sphere of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> and mass <math> <mrow> <mn>8</mn> <mi>π</mi> <mtext> kg</mtext> </mrow> </math> is attached to the lower end of a steel wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> & diameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math>. The wire is suspended from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>22</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> high ceiling of a room. When the sphere is made to swing like a simple pendulum, it just grazes the floor at its lowest point. Calculate the velocity of the sphere at the lowest position. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Y</mi></math> for steel = <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>994</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>11</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math>
questions.solution:
As the length of the wire is 5 m and diameter 2×0.1=0.2 m and at the lowest point, it grazes the floor which is at a distance 5.22 m from the roof, the increase in the length of the wire at lowest point



Δ L = 5 . 2 2 - 5 + 0 . 2

= 0 . 0 2  m

So the tension in the wire (due to elasticity)

T=YALΔL=1.994×1011×π5×10-42×0.025=199.4π N

and as the equation of circular - motion of a mass m tied to a string in a vertical plane is

mv2r=T-mg cosθ

So at the lowest point

mv2r=T-mg as  θ = 0

But here  r = 5 + 0.02 + 0.1 = 5.12 m

So 8πv25.12=199.4π-8π×9.8

i.e., v 2 = 1 2 1 × 5 . 1 2 / 8 = 7 7 . 4 4

So   v = 8.8 m s-1

questions.q: The edge of an aluminium cube is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> long. One face of the cube is firmly fixed to a vertical wall. A mass of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> is then attached to the opposite face of the cube. The shear modulus of aluminium is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>25</mn><mo> </mo><mi>GPa</mi></math>. What is the vertical deflection of this face?
options: 3.92×10-7 m
questions.solution:
Given, side of a cube (l) = 10 cm  = 0.1 m

​Area its each face (A) = l2 = (0.1)2 = 0.01 m2

Load (m) = 100 kg

Tangential force acting on one face of the cube,

​F = mg = 100 × 9.8 = 980 N

Shear stress acting on this face = F A

= 980 0.01 N/m 2

= 9.8 × 104 N/m2

Shear modulus of aluminium (η)) = 25 GPa

= 25 × 109 N/m2

Shear modulus η = Shearing stress Shearing strain

or shearing strain Δ y L = Shearing stress Shear modulus

or Δ y = Shearing stress Shear modulus × L

= 9.8 × 10 4 25 × 10 9 × 0.1

= 0.392 × 10-5 m

= 3.92 × 10-7 m
